The daughter is speaking directly with the kidnapper over the smartphone; he is holding hostage someone she knows personally and demands ¥100 million brought alone by noon, with no police. The father overhears the demand and genuinely does not want the hostage to die, but he refuses to pay.

The reason lies in what paying would set in motion. If the ransom were paid, it would be the daughter—the one dealing directly with the kidnapper—who would personally go to hand over the money. By delivering it she would come face to face with the kidnapper and see his face, leaving her able to identify him; she would then be at grave risk of being killed to silence her as a witness. The father's fear is for the daughter's own life in this delivery, not a belief that the ransom is futile or that refusing saves the hostage (he does not think the hostage will survive without payment). Nor is his decision motivated by any inability of his own or by surveillance, which is irrelevant to the choice.

So although paying might nominally serve the hostage, the father concludes the ransom should not be paid because doing so would send his daughter into the kidnapper's hands, where seeing his face would likely cost her her life. He chooses to keep her from walking into that trap rather than to pay.

runs.latest_final:
The company president had been mugged and thereafter avoided carrying large sums. But an unavoidable situation forced him to carry exactly one million yen in a bag. He feared that if criminals learned the bag held one million yen, they would attack him for it—so he added more of his own cash.

The key, established through the questioning: the one million yen was his own money (Questions 9), and the extra cash served a practical purpose other than merely protecting the money from thieves—specifically it was meant to be seen by another person, in particular a criminal, who would draw a specific conclusion from seeing it (Questions 40, 90, 93, 94). Weight and bulk were irrelevant (Question 77), and the cash was added after the one million yen was already in the bag, not before (Questions 83, 84). All straightforward "make the amount look smaller/different" and "hide the million under decoys" theories were ruled out.

The reconstruction that best fits these confirmed facts: by adding cash so the bag visibly held more than the single, conspicuous million-yen bundle, the president made the bag present itself to any would-be robber as a larger, mixed, ordinary commercial load rather than as the specific one-million-yen prize. The extra cash was there to be *seen*—to shape what a criminal concluded from the bag's visible contents—so that the million yen would no longer stand out as the obvious, targeted sum, and the president would not be singled out for the attack he feared. He traded losing a visible portion of extra cash for not being attacked over the identifiable million.

I acknowledge uncertainty: roughly forty early probes on disguising the amount were rejected, and the exact conclusion the criminal was meant to draw was not fully isolated before the mandatory final. The core explanation rests on the confirmed facts that the added cash was his own, added after the million, practical rather than weight-based, and deliberately meant to be seen by a criminal to change his assessment of the bag.

runs.latest_final:
The hostage is the father himself. He has been abducted and is being held by the kidnapper, who issues the demand over a smartphone: one hundred million yen, brought alone by noon tomorrow, with no police, or the hostage dies. The father is present at the place he is held and hears this demand in real time, while his daughter, who is free and safe, is on the phone begging the kidnapper to spare her father's life.

Because the father is the one in captivity, he cannot deliver the money. The person who would have to bring it is his daughter—and the daughter, out of love for her father, is willing to do it: she would come alone, unprotected, to hand over the ransom in order to save him. But the father understands what that would mean. The kidnapper cannot be trusted to honor the bargain; a criminal holding a hostage and threatening murder would not simply take the money and let her go. Coming alone into his power, the daughter would be at his mercy and could be killed—indeed, she could identify him, giving him an added reason to silence her.

The father therefore reaches a deliberate, self-sacrificing decision. Rather than let his daughter walk into danger and die trying to save him, he decides the ransom should not be paid at all. The danger is not present now—it would arise only from paying—and his refusal is precisely what keeps his daughter from delivering the money and falling into the kidnapper's hands. He knows the kidnapper's threat means refusing likely costs him his own life, but he accepts that price to stop his daughter from sacrificing herself for him.

Thus a tragic reversal of self-sacrifice drives the scene: the daughter is ready to die to save her father, and the father, hearing the demand over the smartphone, chooses his own death instead—deciding that the one hundred million yen should not be paid, so that his daughter will not die for him.

The daughter is genuinely speaking and genuinely in danger, but she is not the hostage: the hostage is a separate person whom both she and her father care about (though apparently not her mother, nor her own child, nor a sibling). A real kidnapper is making the demand over the smartphone: bring one hundred million yen alone by noon tomorrow or the hostage dies, with no police. The father cannot actually raise one hundred million yen by noon, but the decisive reason for his refusal is different.

The daughter is the one who would physically carry and deliver the ransom money to the kidnapper. The handover, however, is a trap — the act of delivering the money is exactly what endangers the hostage and, critically, the daughter. The father realizes that if the ransom were paid, the daughter would be the person sent to the handover and would walk straight into the lethal trap. The hostage would very likely die at that handover regardless, so payment could not save the hostage anyway.

The father's true priority is to protect his daughter: by refusing to pay, no handover is arranged and the daughter is kept out of the dangerous delivery. He knowingly accepts that the hostage may die as the cost of keeping his daughter from rushing into the kidnapper's trap. The scheme is really aimed at victimizing the father — through his money and his family — and he sees that cooperating (paying) is what would actually destroy him and endanger his daughter. So he decides the ransom should not be paid: paying would send his daughter into the trap and would not save the hostage, while refusing keeps her away from it.

In this newly settled Meiji-era village, the dead are buried directly in the forest ground—the village's usual burial ground—and that same forest is where bears range. The father's only daughter died of an illness and was buried there in the ordinary way. Coming into the forest, the father found that a brown bear had dug up her grave and was eating her corpse; he shot the bear and wept over her remains.

Bears are wary of unfamiliar living humans; this bear was scavenging a buried corpse, not hunting a living person, so the danger is not to living villagers. The illness had already caused many villagers to die and be buried in that same forest burial ground, so many other villagers have relatives buried there, exposed to the bears. Because bears will keep digging up and eating bodies buried in that ground—including long-buried remains, not just fresh ones—the father fears that other villagers will suffer exactly what he suffered: bears digging up and eating their buried relatives' bodies, desecrating the dead.

His fear is thus not that bears will kill living people, nor that disease will spread, but that, since the village's dead are buried in bear country, other villagers will also have their relatives' corpses eaten by bears.

runs.latest_final:
The caller is a genuine kidnapper holding the daughter, and the threat is real in form: if unpaid, he threatens to kill her. But the father knows that paying the ransom would directly cause the kidnapper to kill her—the daughter can identify her captor, so once the money changes hands and he no longer needs her, she becomes a dangerous witness whom he must silence. Payment would thus not save her life but seal her death.

At the same time, the father cannot simply deliver the money as demanded. He has himself been lured and confined—trapped where he cannot leave—so he is physically unable to come alone with 100 million yen by noon. His refusal is therefore not a callous rejection but the only sensible response to an impossible demand: compliance would both be impossible on the kidnapper's terms and would give the kidnapper exactly the moment at which to kill the only person who could identify him. The father decides the ransom should not be paid because paying would doom his daughter, while the demand itself cannot be met.

His reasoning centers on the danger of payment rather than any belief that withholding money protects her, and it is not vengeance, a rescue plan, or buying time. The decisive facts are that the daughter can identify the kidnapper—so payment makes her a liability to be eliminated—and that the father is confined and unable to carry out the ransom drop.

runs.latest_final:
The kidnapper has not taken the daughter hostage—the threatened hostage is the father himself. He is held captive by the kidnapper, who is physically present with him and keeping him from leaving, while his daughter is elsewhere on the phone, desperately begging the kidnapper to spare her father's life. The kidnapper demands that 100 million yen be brought alone by noon the next day, with no police.

Because the father is captive and cannot deliver the money himself, the only person who could bring it is the daughter—and she would have to come alone into the kidnapper's hands. The father realizes that if she does this, the kidnapper would harm or kill her too, rather than simply take the money and release anyone; she would be walking into a trap and become a second victim. Paying the ransom would therefore endanger the very person he most wants to protect, while bringing no safety to himself.

So, primarily to keep his daughter from coming alone into the kidnapper's grasp and being harmed, the father tells her not to pay and refuses to have the ransom delivered, accepting his own fate rather than let her place herself in danger.

runs.latest_final:
The father is himself the hostage. A kidnapper is holding him and, over a smartphone, has him listen to his daughter begging for her father's life to be spared while the kidnapper shouts the demand: bring one hundred million yen alone by noon tomorrow, or the hostage dies — no police.

The decisive detail is that the person the kidnapper expects to bring the money is the daughter, and she must come alone. The father realizes this is a trap: if the ransom is paid, the daughter would have to walk into the kidnapper's hands, and the kidnapper would seize or kill her when she arrives. Paying the ransom would therefore not reliably save the father and would put the daughter in deadly danger.

So the father decides the ransom should not be paid. He expects that he himself may die, but he believes that by refusing payment his daughter will stay away and survive. His refusal is a deliberate sacrifice of his own life to keep his daughter out of the kidnapper's hands.
